title: An Empirical Study of Reinforcement Learning Scaling Laws

paper.title: An Empirical Study of Reinforcement Learning Scaling Laws
paper.abstract:
Abstract The discovery of scaling laws enables prediction of the performance , the optimal resource allocation strategy , and the best hyperparameter configuration of a large-scale training job based on inexpensive experiments at smaller scales.
Guided by these empirical scaling laws, the deep learning community has achieved great success in training large (self-)supervised models on Internet-scale datasets.
In contrast, despite its potential and wide application, reinforcement learning (RL) has yet to find a guiding principle for predictable scaling.
In this work, we conduct an empirical study of RL scaling laws of an actor-critic algorithm in two procedurally generated environments, Starpilot and Craftax.
We discover empirical scaling laws with strong predictive performance in both environments. The discovered scaling laws accurately predict the aforementioned three quantities for larger-scale training jobs up to two orders of magnitude in total training compute.
In particular, we employ a variant of Elo scores for the single-agent RL paradigm as an alternative performance metric than the commonly used mean episode return. Our results show that the Elo score is a much more predictable metric than the mean episode return, making it a better choice for fitting scaling laws.
By applying our discovered scaling laws to increase training compute, we establish a new state of the art in the challenging Craftax environment.
Beneath the surface of the global scaling trend, we also observe a non-monotonic scaling pattern of the compute-optimal model size in Craftax. We connect this observation to a pathology known as Ray interference.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: The discovery of empirical scaling laws has revolutionized deep learning, in particular for generative modeling, by transforming model development from a process of heuristic trial-and-error into a predictable engineering discipline ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Hoffmann et al., 2022 ; Bi et al., 2024 ) . Before launching a large-scale training job with a compute budget of C C FLOPs, three critical questions need to be answered ( Muennighoff et al., 2023 ) : (i) (Performance) What is the best achievable performance? (ii) (Allocation) What is the optimal way of allocating the compute budget among axes such as the model size and the dataset size? (iii) (Hyperparameter) What are the optimal hyperparameters for the training job? Scaling laws provide a tool for researchers to answer these questions by conducting inexpensive experiments at smaller scales and extrapolating to larger scales. In contrast to the success of scaling in (self-)supervised learning, reinforcement learning (RL) has yet to find its own guiding principles for predictive scaling. While scaling has powered landmark achievements from game-playing agents ( Silver et al., 2017 ; Vinyals et al., 2019 ; Berner et al., 2019 ) , to fine-tuning large language models ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Khatri et al., 2026 ) , the foundational scaling dynamics of RL remain poorly understood. Unlike (self-)supervised learning, where the data distribution is stationary, RL agents learn from experiences that continuously change as their own policy evolves. Learning in RL is thus inherently non-stationary. This active coupling between policy improvement and data generation implies that RL may be governed by scaling laws distinct from those of passive, supervised regimes. Moreover, unlike the cross entropy loss which has a clear information-theoretical grounding, rewards in RL are often designed in an ad-hoc manner based on heuristics or domain knowledge. Consequently, the common RL performance metric, mean episode return, may not vary smoothly ( Hilton et al., 2023 ) . Due to these differences, it is unclear if the same conclusion, and predictive power, from the (self-)supervised learning scaling laws apply to RL. Existing work on RL scaling laws primarily answer only a subset of the aforementioned three questions while also lacking validation of the predictive performance of the fitted laws ( Jones, 2021 ; Hilton et al., 2023 ; Neumann and Gros, 2023 ) . We argue that the most critical value of scaling laws is in their predictive power and thus validating the predictions is a centerpiece of scaling law studies. In this paper, we present an empirical study of scaling laws in RL. We study all three questions with validation of the predictive performance from small-scale experiments to large-scale experiments in each case. We conduct experiments in two procedurally generated environments, Starpilot ( Cobbe et al., 2020 ) and Craftax ( Matthews et al., 2024 ) . We fit scaling laws for the optimal hyperparameters, model and data sizes, and performance as a function of total training FLOPs C C . We validate the predictive power of the fitted laws by testing their prediction accuracy at one or two orders of magnitude larger training FLOPs. To overcome the non-smoothness of the mean episode return, we employ a variant of the Elo score ( Elo, 1978 ) for the single-agent RL paradigm and showed that it extrapolates effectively whereas the mean episode return does not, making it a critical choice for scaling studies. Our analysis in Craftax reveals that, despite the empirical accuracy of the fitted laws, the compute-optimal frontier does not follow a global log-linear law throughout training. We connect this observation to a phenomenon known as Ray interference ( Schaul et al., 2019 ) . Based on this observation, we argue against the existence of scaling laws for arbitrary RL environments. Our main contributions are: • We establish a two-stage empirical framework for studying RL scaling laws. Our experimental results show that optimal model size and key hyperparameters (e.g., batch size and learning rate) follow predictable power-law relationships with respect to training compute. • We address the non-smoothness of mean episode return and show that a single-agent Elo metric scales log-linearly as a function of training compute, enabling reliable performance extrapolation up to two orders of magnitude. • Guided by our scaling laws, we train an actor-critic agent to 1 ​ e ​ 19 1\text{e}{19} FLOPs and set a new state-of-the-art performance of 54.0 % 54.0\% on the challenging Craftax benchmark. • We identify a local inverse scaling pattern in Craftax and connect it to Ray interference, showing how global trends can mask non-monotonic local dynamics.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: In the past decade, empirical power laws were discovered in multiple deep learning application domains including image classification ( Hestness et al., 2017 ; Rosenfeld et al., 2020 ) , image generation ( Henighan et al., 2020 ) , and language modeling ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . Kaplan et al. (2020) observed that the cross entropy loss of an autoregressive language model scales as a power law with the model size, the dataset size, and the amount of compute used for training across several orders of magnitude. Their work provides a method to answer the performance question. Based on their fitted scaling laws, Kaplan et al. (2020) recommended scaling model size more aggressively than dataset size as training compute increases. Following Kaplan et al. (2020) , Hoffmann et al. (2022) conducted a study on the optimal model size for a certain training compute budget, directly addressing the allocation question. Contradictory to Kaplan et al. (2020) , their work showed that the model size and dataset size should grow at an equal pace while scaling up training compute. In both works, the power laws were fitted to explain the observed data. Their predictions were not validated at larger scales. Moreover, many experimental details such as hyperparameter choices are missing or poorly studied, leaving the hyperparameter question unanswered. To address these limitations, DeepSeek ( Bi et al., 2024 ) studied all three questions of performance, allocation, and hyperparameter and tested the predictive accuracy of the fitted scaling laws at larger scales. Our work builds upon these works. We employed their general methodology to study all three questions and tested the predictive accuracy of the corresponding scaling laws. Meanwhile, our work is different from these works as we focus on RL instead of language modeling. There are few existing works on RL scaling laws. The most closely related work is by Hilton et al. (2023) , who studied scaling laws of single-agent RL. They identified the difficulty of predicting the mean episode return at larger training compute due to its non-smoothness. To address this challenge, they proposed a new metric called intrinsic performance which measures the performance of an RL agent by the minimum amount of training compute needed to achieve parity with it. Although by definition intrinsic performance is not suited for answering the performance question, it served as a tool to answer the allocation question. Fu et al. (2026) studied scaling laws for value-based RL algorithms with a focus on the allocation question and the hyperparameter question. Jones (2021) and Neumann and Gros (2023) studied scaling laws of the AlphaZero agent ( Silver et al., 2017 ) in the context of two-player zero-sum games. Both works found that the Elo ( Elo, 1978 ) of an agent scales predictably with the amount of training compute. Jones (2021) further showed that the Elo scaling law itself scales with the size of the game. Like Hilton et al. (2023) , we focus on the single-agent RL setup. Instead of using intrinsic performance, we employ an Elo variant inspired by Jones (2021) ; Neumann and Gros (2023) as the performance metric which allows us to answer the performance question. In contrast to prior works, which only studied a subset of the three questions, to the best of our knowledge our work is the first to study all three questions in the context of RL, rendering a more complete picture of RL scaling laws. Recently, the success of reasoning models ( Jaech et al., 2024 ; Comanici et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) reinvigorated interest in RL scaling laws in the context of large language model (LLM) finetuning. Examples include Khatri et al. (2026) , Cheng et al. (2026) , and Tan et al. (2026) . These works focus on a specific application domain of RL and concern domain-specific quantities such as the number of parallel rollouts per prompt and the pass rate on a specific dataset. In contrast, our work focuses on the more general sequential-decision making setup with minimum assumptions about the environment and the reward structures.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: Our methodology implements a two-stage framework adapted from the paradigm proposed by Bi et al. (2024) . First, we characterize hyperparameter scaling dynamics by conducting a systematic grid search across small-to-medium compute budgets to establish empirical power laws that parameterize optimal configurations as functions of training compute. Second, we determine the joint scaling behavior of model size and performance using the isoFLOPs profile approach ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) , dynamically configuring the hyperparameters in this stage using the optimal values prescribed by our first-stage scaling laws. To validate this framework, we first conduct a rigorous scientific evaluation of predictive performance at a 10 × 10\times compute frontier by independently comparing each scaling law’s prediction against the empirical ground truth. We then showcase the practical utility of these scaling laws at a 100 × 100\times compute scale, mirroring real-world constraints where validating prediction accuracy is computationally prohibitive. Rather than evaluating the laws themselves, this step demonstrates their use in practice: we execute a large-scale training run configured by our hyperparameter and model size prescriptions, comparing its realized performance to the performance scaling law’s prediction to verify that the high-budget training job meets expectation.

sections.heading: 3.1 Hyperparameter scaling laws
sections.text: We used the A2C algorithm ( Mnih et al., 2016 ) across all experiments in this work. In addition to batch size and learning rate, the entropy regularization strength is also an important hyperparameter in A2C. We did a preliminary grid search over combinations of these three hyperparameters at a low compute regime. The optimal entropy regularization strength is consistent across different compute budgets. Following this observation, we decided to focus on studying the scaling dynamics of batch size and learning rate. Specifically, we fixed the rollout length of each trajectory and varied batch size by changing the number of parallel environment instances. To characterize the scaling dynamics of hyperparameters, we first need to find their optimal values for a set of different training budgets at a small scale. For each training FLOPs C C , we conduct a grid search on batch size and learning rate across a few different model sizes to identify their optimal values. Due to randomness in the training process, the empirical performance is a noisy estimate of the true performance. Thus the empirical optimal hyperparameter configuration is often not the true optimum. RL performance evaluation is known to suffer from higher variance than supervised learning ( Henderson et al., 2018 ) , which makes the identification problem even harder. To reduce the variance of the empirical performance measurement, we conduct multiple independent jobs for each configuration with different random seeds. We then aggregate the episode returns across random seeds by their interquartile mean (IQM). Moreover, to take into account the randomness of the empirical results, we do bootstrapping by resampling the random seeds for the experiments. For each resampling, we pick the batch size and learning rate that yields the highest IQM of the episode return. We call this configuration a competitive configuration. Through bootstrapping, we obtain a set of competitive configurations for each training compute C C . Instead of fitting the empirically optimal configurations, we fit power laws to all competitive configurations in the following forms: B ∗ ​ ( C ) \displaystyle B^{*}(C) = a B ​ C d B \displaystyle=a_{B}C^{d_{B}} (1) α ∗ ​ ( C ) \displaystyle\alpha^{*}(C) = a α ​ C d α \displaystyle=a_{\alpha}C^{d_{\alpha}} (2) B ∗ ​ ( C ) B^{*}(C) and α ∗ ​ ( C ) \alpha^{*}(C) represent the average competitive batch size and learning rate at training FLOPs C C respectively. a B a_{B} , d B d_{B} , a α a_{\alpha} , and d α d_{\alpha} are parameters fitted from the data. Bi et al. (2024) employ a method that shares the same spirit as ours to combat the noise in optimal hyperparameter identification. They define “near-optimal” hyperparameters as the ones that yield a loss within 0.25 % 0.25\% of the empirical minimum. Similar to our method, they then fit the scaling laws to the near-optimal hyperparameters. We do not use the same method because unlike cross entropy the episode return need not vary smoothly through training. It is hard to pick a threshold for the “near-optimal” definition. Instead, we rely on bootstrapping to address randomness in experiments.

sections.heading: 3.2 Allocation scaling laws
sections.text: To understand the optimal allocation of training compute, we first need to calculate the total FLOPs C C of a training run. In Transformer-based language models, this is often approximated by C = 6 ​ N ​ D C=6ND where N N denotes the total number of parameters in the model and D D denotes the total number of tokens consumed during training ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . This approximation is based on dense layers. However, we use convolutional networks which do not follow the same calculation. Therefore, similar to the FLOPs-per-token notion used by Bi et al. (2024) , we use FLOPs-per-frame (FPF), denoted by M M , as a measurement of the model size. Here a frame refers to the observation of a single step in the environment. FPF is defined as the number of FLOPs spent on each observation during training. The total training compute is thus C = M ​ D C=MD where D D denotes the number of frames the agent is trained for. Note that for a model-based RL agent we may need to take additional factors such as planning steps into account. We focus on model-free RL agents in this work and leave the study of model-based agents to future work. With the clear factoring of training FLOPs, we use the isoFLOPs profile approach ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) to study the optimal compute allocation between model size and data size. We need to find the optimal allocation at a set of different training FLOPs at small scale. For each training FLOPs C C , we train models of different sizes using hyperparameters predicted by their corresponding scaling laws. To combat variance, we run multiple independent jobs for each model size with different random seeds and aggregate the results by IQM. Then we fit a parabola to approximate the mapping from FPF to performance. We extract the optimum of the parabola to identify the optimal FPF M ∗ M^{*} for training FLOPs C C . Lastly, we fit a power law in the following form: M ∗ ​ ( C ) = a M ​ C d M \displaystyle M^{*}(C)=a_{M}C^{d_{M}} (3) a M a_{M} and d M d_{M} are parameters fitted from data. We do not need to fit a separate law for the optimal data size D ∗ D^{*} as it can be derived from M ∗ M^{*} .

sections.heading: 3.3 Performance scaling laws in Elo
sections.text: Before predicting the performance as a function of the training compute, we must first determine how performance is measured. As observed by Hilton et al. (2023) , the compute-optimal frontier need not vary smoothly when the performance is measured in mean episode return. The fundamental reason is that the magnitude of rewards (and thus returns) does not track learning progress continuously. To address this problem, we employ a variant of the Elo score ( Elo, 1978 ) as a performance measurement of a single-agent RL training system. Elo is typically used to measure the relative playing strength of different players within a league in two-player games. In this experiment, the league consists of the final agent checkpoint of each training run. We compute the Elo for each agent in our single-agent environment by creating simulated two-player games. We reserve a fixed set of environment instances for evaluation. Every agent is evaluated on this evaluation set. We then set up a simulated tournament between every pair of agents. For each pair, we treat each evaluation environment as an independent competition where the agent that achieved a higher return wins. If both agents achieve the same score, it is a tie and counts 0.5 0.5 win for each agent. By aggregating over the entire evaluation set, we compute a win rate of one agent against the other. We do this for every pair of agents in the league and obtain a win rate matrix where cell ( i , j ) (i,j) denotes the win rate of agent i i against agent j j . By fitting a Bradley-Terry model ( Bradley and Terry, 1952 ) to this win rate matrix, we obtain an Elo score for each agent. Note that Elo is a relative metric and thus the solution is not unique. To anchor it, we subtract every agent’s Elo by the Elo of the random policy post hoc. For the performance scaling laws, we use the same data from the allocation experiment. We solve the parabola to find the optimal performance for each training compute C C and fitted a scaling law in Elo. Since the Elo score itself is already in log-scale, instead of a power law, we fit a log-linear law in the form below where d Elo d_{\text{Elo}} and a Elo a_{\text{Elo}} are parameters fitted from data: Elo ∗ ​ ( C ) = d Elo ​ log 10 ​ C + a Elo \displaystyle\text{Elo}^{*}(C)=d_{\text{Elo}}\log_{10}{C}+a_{\text{Elo}} (4)

sections.heading: 4.4 Inverse scaling analysis
sections.text: In Craftax, we observed a double-crossover between 3 ​ e ​ 13 3\text{e}{13} and 1 ​ e ​ 15 1\text{e}{15} FLOPs, demonstrating a local inverse scaling pattern where a smaller model outperforms a larger model as the training budget increases. The left plot in Figure 5 shows this phenomenon. The bigger model outperforms the smaller model at 1 ​ e ​ 14 1\text{e}{14} FLOPs but underperforms at 3 ​ e ​ 14 3\text{e}{14} FLOPs. Eventually at 1 ​ e ​ 15 1\text{e}{15} the bigger model performs better again. This observation contradicts the common belief that the optimal model size grows monotonically as we scale up training compute. We conjecture that this phenomenon stems from a specific design of the game dynamics and the pathological learning dynamics it incurs. In Craftax, the agent must defeat at least 8 8 enemies on each level to unlock the door to the next level. This rule applies to every level except the first, on which the door to the second level (the “dungeon”) is always open from the beginning of the episode, rendering battling optional. However, defeating enemies is relatively easier than entering the dungeon because the door is always located at the center of a “mountain”, surrounded by stones. Consequently, the agent learns to defeat enemies before switching to entering the dungeon. During the transition, it stops defeating enemies because it is unnecessary though rewarding. In other words, as the experience accumulates, the agent learns to master the more rewarding skill of entering the dungeon while forgetting the less rewarding skill of battling. These learning dynamics differ drastically from the supervised learning setting where the model needs to fit a growing set of data, which naturally demands more capacity. In this case, however, the agent can reallocate the model capacity from battling to path finding without growing the model size. The smaller model then has an advantage over the larger model because it sees more data under the same compute budget. Our conjecture is supported by the achievements the agent unlocked during training, shown in the right plot of Figure 5 . Up to 1 ​ e ​ 14 1\text{e}{14} FLOPs, the agent has little success in entering the dungeon regardless of its model size. Progress mainly comes from better battling skills. However, at 3 ​ e ​ 14 3\text{e}{14} FLOPs, the agent learns to enter the dungeon while avoiding battles at the same time. Instead of growing its skill set, which demands more model capacity, the agent switches from one skill to another, giving the smaller model advantages. This pathology of one reward source suppressing the learning signal from another reward source during the early phase of training resembles Ray interference ( Schaul et al., 2019 ) . It is a product of the interaction between the environment dynamics and the learning dynamics. Therefore, a different learning algorithm than actor-critic may demonstrate a different scaling behavior. We leave the comparison of the scaling properties of different algorithms to future work. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we presented a systematic empirical study of scaling laws in RL, investigating hyperparameter configuration, compute allocation, and performance prediction across the Starpilot and Craftax environments. We established that optimal hyperparameters follow power-law relationships with respect to total training compute. Furthermore, we also characterized the optimal allocation between model size and data size as functions of training FLOPs. To address the non-smoothness of mean episode return, we employed a single-agent variant of the Elo score. We demonstrated that the Elo score scales predictably, enabling robust performance extrapolation up to two orders of magnitude in training compute. Guided by these scaling laws, we scaled up a simple actor-critic algorithm to 1 ​ e ​ 19 1\text{e}{19} training FLOPs and achieved a new state-of-the-art performance of 54.0 % 54.0\% in the challenging Craftax benchmark. However, our analysis also uncovered a local inverse scaling pathology in Craftax, which we connected to a pathology known as Ray interference, illustrating that global scaling trends can obscure non-monotonic local dynamics. Despite these contributions, several limitations remain to be addressed in future work. First, our empirical study was restricted to a single model-free actor-critic algorithm (A2C); further research is required to verify if our findings generalize to other RL algorithms such as value-based or model-based algorithms. Second, while the Elo score offers predictable mathematical scaling, it is fundamentally a relative metric within a closed league of evaluated agents, lacking direct semantic grounding to the underlying task. Consequently, in domains where rewards carry critical semantic meanings, Elo-based scaling laws may be less effective at providing informative or absolute performance predictions. Finally, our discovery of Ray interference in Craftax indicates that RL scaling is highly sensitive to the specific alignment of environmental dynamics and reward structures, suggesting that a single, universal scaling law may not apply across all arbitrary RL environments. Designing algorithms resilient to Ray interference remains a critical avenue for future research.

sections.heading: Appendix A Training Algorithm Details
sections.text: In both Starpilot and Craftax, we train agents using the A2C ( Mnih et al., 2016 ) algorithm.

sections.heading: A.1 Neural Network Architectures.
sections.text: In Starpilot experiments, we use the IMPALA ( Espeholt et al., 2018 ) residual convolutional neural network architecture ( He et al., 2016 ) with a shared torso between the policy and the value function. Layer normalization ( Ba et al., 2016 ) is applied between every layer and its following activation function. We vary the model size by the number of convolutional channels of the first layer. The width of subsequent layers scale proportionally. In Craftax we use the symbolic observations. We apply a 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolutional layer with E E channels to the map grid. We then flatten the grid and apply a linear layer with dimension H = 16 ​ E H=16E to compress the map to a compact vector representation. The inventory is encoded to a vector of the same dimensionality H H by a linear layer. We fuse the map and the inventory by adding their vectors together. Note that we apply layer normalization to their vectors independently before fusion. The fused vector is fed into an LSTM ( Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997 ) cell with H H hidden units to handle partial observability. Lastly, we apply linear layers to the output of the LSTM cell to map the state representation to the policy logits and the value function. We used GELU ( Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016 ) activation. Similarly, we apply layer normalization before every activation layer. We control the model size by varying the number of channels in the 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolutional layer E E .

sections.heading: A.2 Hyperparameters
sections.text: In Starpilot experiments, we use a discount factor of 0.999 0.999 . We set the rollout length to a constant 16 16 . The weight for the value function loss is 0.5 0.5 and the entropy regularization strength is 0.01 0.01 . We use the Adam ( Kingma and Ba, 2015 ) optimizer with β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{2}=0.999 , and ϵ = 1 ​ e − 8 \epsilon=1\text{e}{-8} . The learning rate is linearly decayed to 0 0 through training. We clip the gradient by global norm to 0.5 0.5 . In Craftax, we use a discount factor of 0.999 0.999 . We set the rollout length to a constant 16 16 . We break each batch of rollouts into 4 4 minibatches and thus apply 4 4 gradient updates per batch. We do minibatching to improve the overall throughput of the training system because we can employ more parallel environments. The batch size in Section 4 is the number of observations in each minibatch. We apply VTrace ( Espeholt et al., 2018 ) to handle off-policyness caused by minibatch. The weight for the value function loss is 0.5 0.5 and the entropy regularization strength is 0.001 0.001 . We use the Adam ( Kingma and Ba, 2015 ) optimizer with β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.99 \beta_{2}=0.99 , and ϵ = 1 ​ e − 8 \epsilon=1\text{e}{-8} . The learning rate is linearly decayed to 0 0 through training. We clip the gradient by global norm to 0.5 0.5 . In both environments, we reserved 1024 1024 instances for evaluation.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.33420v1 [cs.LG] 24 Oct 2026 An Empirical Study of Reinforcement Learning Scaling Laws Zeyu Zheng Clare Lyle Khimya Khetarpal & Will Dabney Affiliation: Google DeepMind Email: {zeyuzheng,clarelyle,khimya,wdabney}@google.com Abstract The discovery of scaling laws enables prediction of the performance , the optimal resource allocation strategy , and the best hyperparameter configuration of a large-scale training job based on inexpensive experiments at smaller scales. Guided by these empirical scaling laws, the deep learning community has achieved great success in training large (self-)supervised models on Internet-scale datasets. In contrast, despite its potential and wide application, reinforcement learning (RL) has yet to find a guiding principle for predictable scaling. In this work, we conduct an empirical study of RL scaling laws of an actor-critic algorithm in two procedurally generated environments, Starpilot and Craftax. We discover empirical scaling laws with strong predictive performance in both environments. The discovered scaling laws accurately predict the aforementioned three quantities for larger-scale training jobs up to two orders of magnitude in total training compute. In particular, we employ a variant of Elo scores for the single-agent RL paradigm as an alternative performance metric than the commonly used mean episode return. Our results show that the Elo score is a much more predictable metric than the mean episode return, making it a better choice for fitting scaling laws. By applying our discovered scaling laws to increase training compute, we establish a new state of the art in the challenging Craftax environment. Beneath the surface of the global scaling trend, we also observe a non-monotonic scaling pattern of the compute-optimal model size in Craftax. We connect this observation to a pathology known as Ray interference. 1 Introduction The discovery of empirical scaling laws has revolutionized deep learning, in particular for generative modeling, by transforming model development from a process of heuristic trial-and-error into a predictable engineering discipline ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Hoffmann et al., 2022 ; Bi et al., 2024 ) . Before launching a large-scale training job with a compute budget of C C FLOPs, three critical questions need to be answered ( Muennighoff et al., 2023 ) : (i) (Performance) What is the best achievable performance? (ii) (Allocation) What is the optimal way of allocating the compute budget among axes such as the model size and the dataset size? (iii) (Hyperparameter) What are the optimal hyperparameters for the training job? Scaling laws provide a tool for researchers to answer these questions by conducting inexpensive experiments at smaller scales and extrapolating to larger scales. In contrast to the success of scaling in (self-)supervised learning, reinforcement learning (RL) has yet to find its own guiding principles for predictive scaling. While scaling has powered landmark achievements from game-playing agents ( Silver et al., 2017 ; Vinyals et al., 2019 ; Berner et al., 2019 ) , to fine-tuning large language models ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Khatri et al., 2026 ) , the foundational scaling dynamics of RL remain poorly understood. Unlike (self-)supervised learning, where the data distribution is stationary, RL agents learn from experiences that continuously change as their own policy evolves. Learning in RL is thus inherently non-stationary. This active coupling between policy improvement and data generation implies that RL may be governed by scaling laws distinct from those of passive, supervised regimes. Moreover, unlike the cross entropy loss which has a clear information-theoretical grounding, rewards in RL are often designed in an ad-hoc manner based on heuristics or domain knowledge. Consequently, the common RL performance metric, mean episode return, may not vary smoothly ( Hilton et al., 2023 ) . Due to these differences, it is unclear if the same conclusion, and predictive power, from the (self-)supervised learning scaling laws apply to RL. Existing work on RL scaling laws primarily answer only a subset of the aforementioned three questions while also lacking validation of the predictive performance of the fitted laws ( Jones, 2021 ; Hilton et al., 2023 ; Neumann and Gros, 2023 ) . We argue that the most critical value of scaling laws is in their predictive power and thus validating the predictions is a centerpiece of scaling law studies. In this paper, we present an empirical study of scaling laws in RL. We study all three questions with validation of the predictive performance from small-scale experiments to large-scale experiments in each case. We conduct experiments in two procedurally generated environments, Starpilot ( Cobbe et al., 2020 ) and Craftax ( Matthews et al., 2024 ) . We fit scaling laws for the optimal hyperparameters, model and data sizes, and performance as a function of total training FLOPs C C . We validate the predictive power of the fitted laws by testing their prediction accuracy at one or two orders of magnitude larger training FLOPs. To overcome the non-smoothness of the mean episode return, we employ a variant of the Elo score ( Elo, 1978 ) for the single-agent RL paradigm and showed that it extrapolates effectively whereas the mean episode return does not, making it a critical choice for scaling studies. Our analysis in Craftax reveals that, despite the empirical accuracy of the fitted laws, the compute-optimal frontier does not follow a global log-linear law throughout training. We connect this observation to a phenomenon known as Ray interference ( Schaul et al., 2019 ) . Based on this observation, we argue against the existence of scaling laws for arbitrary RL environments. Our main contributions are: • We establish a two-stage empirical framework for studying RL scaling laws. Our experimental results show that optimal model size and key hyperparameters (e.g., batch size and learning rate) follow predictable power-law relationships with respect to training compute. • We address the non-smoothness of mean episode return and show that a single-agent Elo metric scales log-linearly as a function of training compute, enabling reliable performance extrapolation up to two orders of magnitude. • Guided by our scaling laws, we train an actor-critic agent to 1 ​ e ​ 19 1\text{e}{19} FLOPs and set a new state-of-the-art performance of 54.0 % 54.0\% on the challenging Craftax benchmark. • We identify a local inverse scaling pattern in Craftax and connect it to Ray interference, showing how global trends can mask non-monotonic local dynamics. 2 Related Work In the past decade, empirical power laws were discovered in multiple deep learning application domains including image classification ( Hestness et al., 2017 ; Rosenfeld et al., 2020 ) , image generation ( Henighan et al., 2020 ) , and language modeling ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . Kaplan et al. (2020) observed that the cross entropy loss of an autoregressive language model scales as a power law with the model size, the dataset size, and the amount of compute used for training across several orders of magnitude. Their work provides a method to answer the performance question. Based on their fitted scaling laws, Kaplan et al. (2020) recommended scaling model size more aggressively than dataset size as training compute increases. Following Kaplan et al. (2020) , Hoffmann et al. (2022) conducted a study on the optimal model size for a certain training compute budget, directly addressing the allocation question. Contradictory to Kaplan et al. (2020) , their work showed that the model size and dataset size should grow at an equal pace while scaling up training compute. In both works, the power laws were fitted to explain the observed data. Their predictions were not validated at larger scales. Moreover, many experimental details such as hyperparameter choices are missing or poorly studied, leaving the hyperparameter question unanswered. To address these limitations, DeepSeek ( Bi et al., 2024 ) studied all three questions of performance, allocation, and hyperparameter and tested the predictive accuracy of the fitted scaling laws at larger scales. Our work builds upon these works. We employed their general methodology to study all three questions and tested the predictive accuracy of the corresponding scaling laws. Meanwhile, our work is different from these works as we focus on RL instead of language modeling. There are few existing works on RL scaling laws. The most closely related work is by Hilton et al. (2023) , who studied scaling laws of single-agent RL. They identified the difficulty of predicting the mean episode return at larger training compute due to its non-smoothness. To address this challenge, they proposed a new metric called intrinsic performance which measures the performance of an RL agent by the minimum amount of training compute needed to achieve parity with it. Although by definition intrinsic performance is not suited for answering the performance question, it served as a tool to answer the allocation question. Fu et al. (2026) studied scaling laws for value-based RL algorithms with a focus on the allocation question and the hyperparameter question. Jones (2021) and Neumann and Gros (2023) studied scaling laws of the AlphaZero agent ( Silver et al., 2017 ) in the context of two-player zero-sum games. Both works found that the Elo ( Elo, 1978 ) of an agent scales predictably with the amount of training compute. Jones (2021) further showed that the Elo scaling law itself scales with the size of the game. Like Hilton et al. (2023) , we focus on the single-agent RL setup. Instead of using intrinsic performance, we employ an Elo variant inspired by Jones (2021) ; Neumann and Gros (2023) as the performance metric which allows us to answer the performance question. In contrast to prior works, which only studied a subset of the three questions, to the best of our knowledge our work is the first to study all three questions in the context of RL, rendering a more complete picture of RL scaling laws. Recently, the success of reasoning models ( Jaech et al., 2024 ; Comanici et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) reinvigorated interest in RL scaling laws in the context of large language model (LLM) finetuning. Examples include Khatri et al. (2026) , Cheng et al. (2026) , and Tan et al. (2026) . These works focus on a specific application domain of RL and concern domain-specific quantities such as the number of parallel rollouts per prompt and the pass rate on a specific dataset. In contrast, our work focuses on the more general sequential-decision making setup with minimum assumptions about the environment and the reward structures. 3 Method Our methodology implements a two-stage framework adapted from the paradigm proposed by Bi et al. (2024) . First, we characterize hyperparameter scaling dynamics by conducting a systematic grid search across small-to-medium compute budgets to establish empirical power laws that parameterize optimal configurations as functions of training compute. Second, we determine the joint scaling behavior of model size and performance using the isoFLOPs profile approach ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) , dynamically configuring the hyperparameters in this stage using the optimal values prescribed by our first-stage scaling laws. To validate this framework, we first conduct a rigorous scientific evaluation of predictive performance at a 10 × 10\times compute frontier by independently comparing each scaling law’s prediction against the empirical ground truth. We then showcase the practical utility of these scaling laws at a 100 × 100\times compute scale, mirroring real-world constraints where validating prediction accuracy is computationally prohibitive. Rather than evaluating the laws themselves, this step demonstrates their use in practice: we execute a large-scale training run configured by our hyperparameter and model size prescriptions, comparing its realized performance to the performance scaling law’s prediction to verify that the high-budget training job meets expectation. 3.1 Hyperparameter scaling laws We used the A2C algorithm ( Mnih et al., 2016 ) across all experiments in this work. In addition to batch size and learning rate, the entropy regularization strength is also an important hyperparameter in A2C. We did a preliminary grid search over combinations of these three hyperparameters at a low compute regime. The optimal entropy regularization strength is consistent across different compute budgets. Following this observation, we decided to focus on studying the scaling dynamics of batch size and learning rate. Specifically, we fixed the rollout length of each trajectory and varied batch size by changing the number of parallel environment instances. To characterize the scaling dynamics of hyperparameters, we first need to find their optimal values for a set of different training budgets at a small scale. For each training FLOPs C C , we conduct a grid search on batch size and learning rate across a few different model sizes to identify their optimal values. Due to randomness in the training process, the empirical performance is a noisy estimate of the true performance. Thus the empirical optimal hyperparameter configuration is often not the true optimum. RL performance evaluation is known to suffer from higher variance than supervised learning ( Henderson et al., 2018 ) , which makes the identification problem even harder. To reduce the variance of the empirical performance measurement, we conduct multiple independent jobs for each configuration with different random seeds. We then aggregate the episode returns across random seeds by their interquartile mean (IQM). Moreover, to take into account the randomness of the empirical results, we do bootstrapping by resampling the random seeds for the experiments. For each resampling, we pick the batch size and learning rate that yields the highest IQM of the episode return. We call this configuration a competitive configuration. Through bootstrapping, we obtain a set of competitive configurations for each training compute C C . Instead of fitting the empirically optimal configurations, we fit power laws to all competitive configurations in the following forms: B ∗ ​ ( C ) \displaystyle B^{*}(C) = a B ​ C d B \displaystyle=a_{B}C^{d_{B}} (1) α ∗ ​ ( C ) \displaystyle\alpha^{*}(C) = a α ​ C d α \displaystyle=a_{\alpha}C^{d_{\alpha}} (2) B ∗ ​ ( C ) B^{*}(C) and α ∗ ​ ( C ) \alpha^{*}(C) represent the average competitive batch size and learning rate at training FLOPs C C respectively. a B a_{B} , d B d_{B} , a α a_{\alpha} , and d α d_{\alpha} are parameters fitted from the data. Bi et al. (2024) employ a method that shares the same spirit as ours to combat the noise in optimal hyperparameter identification. They define “near-optimal” hyperparameters as the ones that yield a loss within 0.25 % 0.25\% of the empirical minimum. Similar to our method, they then fit the scaling laws to the near-optimal hyperparameters. We do not use the same method because unlike cross entropy the episode return need not vary smoothly through training. It is hard to pick a threshold for the “near-optimal” definition. Instead, we rely on bootstrapping to address randomness in experiments. 3.2 Allocation scaling laws To understand the optimal allocation of training compute, we first need to calculate the total FLOPs C C of a training run. In Transformer-based language models, this is often approximated by C = 6 ​ N ​ D C=6ND where N N denotes the total number of parameters in the model and D D denotes the total number of tokens consumed during training ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . This approximation is based on dense layers. However, we use convolutional networks which do not follow the same calculation. Therefore, similar to the FLOPs-per-token notion used by Bi et al. As observed by Hilton et al. (2023) , the compute-optimal frontier need not vary smoothly when the performance is measured in mean episode return. The fundamental reason is that the magnitude of rewards (and thus returns) does not track learning progress continuously. To address this problem, we employ a variant of the Elo score ( Elo, 1978 ) as a performance measurement of a single-agent RL training system. Elo is typically used to measure the relative playing strength of different players within a league in two-player games. In this experiment, the league consists of the final agent checkpoint of each training run. We compute the Elo for each agent in our single-agent environment by creating simulated two-player games. We reserve a fixed set of environment instances for evaluation. Every agent is evaluated on this evaluation set. We then set up a simulated tournament between every pair of agents. For each pair, we treat each evaluation environment as an independent competition where the agent that achieved a higher return wins. If both agents achieve the same score, it is a tie and counts 0.5 0.5 win for each agent. By aggregating over the entire evaluation set, we compute a win rate of one agent against the other. The left plot in Figure 5 shows this phenomenon. The bigger model outperforms the smaller model at 1 ​ e ​ 14 1\text{e}{14} FLOPs but underperforms at 3 ​ e ​ 14 3\text{e}{14} FLOPs. Eventually at 1 ​ e ​ 15 1\text{e}{15} the bigger model performs better again. This observation contradicts the common belief that the optimal model size grows monotonically as we scale up training compute. We conjecture that this phenomenon stems from a specific design of the game dynamics and the pathological learning dynamics it incurs. In Craftax, the agent must defeat at least 8 8 enemies on each level to unlock the door to the next level. This rule applies to every level except the first, on which the door to the second level (the “dungeon”) is always open from the beginning of the episode, rendering battling optional. However, defeating enemies is relatively easier than entering the dungeon because the door is always located at the center of a “mountain”, surrounded by stones. Consequently, the agent learns to defeat enemies before switching to entering the dungeon. During the transition, it stops defeating enemies because it is unnecessary though rewarding. In other words, as the experience accumulates, the agent learns to master the more rewarding skill of entering the dungeon while forgetting the less rewarding skill of battling. These learning dynamics differ drastically from the supervised learning setting where the model needs to fit a growing set of data, which naturally demands more capacity. In this case, however, the agent can reallocate the model capacity from battling to path finding without growing the model size. The smaller model then has an advantage over the larger model because it sees more data under the same compute budget. Our conjecture is supported by the achievements the agent unlocked during training, shown in the right plot of Figure 5 . Up to 1 ​ e ​ 14 1\text{e}{14} FLOPs, the agent has little success in entering the dungeon regardless of its model size. Progress mainly comes from better battling skills. However, at 3 ​ e ​ 14 3\text{e}{14} FLOPs, the agent learns to enter the dungeon while avoiding battles at the same time. Instead of growing its skill set, which demands more model capacity, the agent switches from one skill to another, giving the smaller model advantages. This pathology of one reward source suppressing the learning signal from another reward source during the early phase of training resembles Ray interference ( Schaul et al., 2019 ) . It is a product of the interaction between the environment dynamics and the learning dynamics. Therefore, a different learning algorithm than actor-critic may demonstrate a different scaling behavior. We leave the comparison of the scaling properties of different algorithms to future work. Error bars show the standard error across 5 5 random seeds. 5 Conclusion In this work, we presented a systematic empirical study of scaling laws in RL, investigating hyperparameter configuration, compute allocation, and performance prediction across the Starpilot and Craftax environments. We established that optimal hyperparameters follow power-law relationships with respect to total training compute. Furthermore, we also characterized the optimal allocation between model size and data size as functions of training FLOPs. To address the non-smoothness of mean episode return, we employed a single-agent variant of the Elo score. We demonstrated that the Elo score scales predictably, enabling robust performance extrapolation up to two orders of magnitude in training compute. Guided by these scaling laws, we scaled up a simple actor-critic algorithm to 1 ​ e ​ 19 1\text{e}{19} training FLOPs and achieved a new state-of-the-art performance of 54.0 % 54.0\% in the challenging Craftax benchmark. However, our analysis also uncovered a local inverse scaling pathology in Craftax, which we connected to a pathology known as Ray interference, illustrating that global scaling trends can obscure non-monotonic local dynamics. Despite these contributions, several limitations remain to be addressed in future work. First, our empirical study was restricted to a single model-free actor-critic algorithm (A2C); further research is required to verify if our findings generalize to other RL algorithms such as value-based or model-based algorithms. Second, while the Elo score offers predictable mathematical scaling, it is fundamentally a relative metric within a closed league of evaluated agents, lacking direct semantic grounding to the underlying task. Consequently, in domains where rewards carry critical semantic meanings, Elo-based scaling laws may be less effective at providing informative or absolute performance predictions. Finally, our discovery of Ray interference in Craftax indicates that RL scaling is highly sensitive to the specific alignment of environmental dynamics and reward structures, suggesting that a single, universal scaling law may not apply across all arbitrary RL environments. Designing algorithms resilient to Ray interference remains a critical avenue for future research.
